claims.text: Axillary nerve origin: one of the two terminal branches of the posterior cord, from C5 and C6.
claims.quote: The axillary nerve is one of two terminal branches of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. It receives contributions from C5 and C6 nerve roots.

claims.text: Axillary nerve course: runs behind the axillary artery, passes below the shoulder joint and leaves the axilla through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery.
claims.quote: Lying posteriorly to the axillary artery in the axilla, it passes inferiorly to the shoulder joint, exiting the axilla through the quadrangular space, with the posterior circumflex humeral artery, to supply the deltoid muscle and a small patch of overlying skin.

claims.text: Axillary nerve supply: deltoid and teres minor; the glenohumeral joint; skin over the deltoid (superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm).
claims.quote: muscular branches: deltoid and teres minor muscles articular branches to the glenohumeral joint superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm: skin overlying the deltoid muscle

claims.text: Axillary nerve injury: anterior shoulder dislocation can injure it, giving decreased sensation over the deltoid.
claims.quote: With an anterior dislocation, the acromion is prominent, and the elbow is held slightly out from the side in abduction. The humeral head is displaced anteriorly and inferiorly and cannot be palpated in its usual position. Patients are unwilling to move the arm. They may have motor and sensory deficits (eg, if the axillary nerve is injured, decreased sensation over the deltoid).

claims.text: Musculocutaneous nerve origin: a terminal branch of the lateral cord (alongside the lateral root of the median nerve), from C5–7.
claims.quote: The musculocutaneous nerve is one of two terminal branches of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus (along with the lateral root of the median nerve). It receives fibers from the C5-7 nerve roots.

claims.text: Musculocutaneous nerve course: pierces and supplies coracobrachialis, descends between biceps brachii and brachialis, and continues past the elbow as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (its sensory continuation).
claims.quote: In the axilla, the musculocutaneous nerve courses laterally away from the axillary artery, pierces (and supplies) the coracobrachialis muscle and descends towards the elbow between biceps brachii and brachialis muscles. In the cubital fossa, it courses lateral to the biceps tendon as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which is simply the sensory continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve after it has distributed all its motor fibers in the anterior compartment of the arm.

claims.text: Musculocutaneous nerve supply: coracobrachialis, biceps brachii and brachialis; the shoulder and elbow joints; skin of the lateral forearm.
claims.quote: muscular branches: anterior compartment of the arm (coracobrachialis, biceps brachii and brachialis muscles) articular branches: shoulder and elbow joints lateral cutaneous: lateral aspect of the forearm

claims.text: Radial nerve origin: one of the two terminal branches of the posterior cord, from C5–T1.
claims.quote: The radial nerve is one of two terminal branches of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. It receives contributions from C5-T1 nerve roots.

claims.text: Radial nerve course: winds around the spiral groove of the humerus with the profunda brachii artery, pierces the lateral intermuscular septum at mid-humerus, passes in front of the lateral epicondyle and divides in the cubital fossa into superficial and deep branches.
claims.quote: In the posterior compartment of the arm, it winds its way around the spiral groove of the humerus, accompanying profunda brachii artery. It pierces the lateral intermuscular septum at the midpoint of the humerus to enter the anterior compartment of the arm. It lies deep to the upper brachialis and then brachioradialis. It passes to the forearm by coursing anterior to the lateral epicondyle at the level of the elbow joint. It enters the cubital fossa, where it divides into superficial and deep branches.

claims.text: Radial nerve supply in the arm: triceps brachii, anconeus, brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus.
claims.quote: muscular twigs in the arm: triceps brachii, anconeus, brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus muscles

claims.text: Deep branch / posterior interosseous nerve: the deep branch supplies extensor carpi radialis brevis and supinator, then continues as the posterior interosseous nerve to extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor indicis, extensor pollicis longus and brevis, and abductor pollicis longus.
claims.quote: deep branch of the radial nerve: direct innervation to the extensor carpi radialis brevis and supinator muscles continues as the posterior interosseous nerve to supply the deep extensors of the dorsal arm (extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor indicis, extensor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, abductor pollicis longus)

claims.text: Superficial radial nerve: sensation to the dorsum of the hand, the dorsal first to third digits and the dorsal lateral fourth finger, sparing the fingertips.
claims.quote: superficial branch of the radial nerve: supplies cutaneous sensation to the dorsal aspect of the hand, dorsal aspect of the first to third digits and the dorsal lateral aspect of the fourth finger (sparing the finger tips)

claims.text: Radial palsy look-alike: C7 radiculopathy can cause motor deficits similar to radial nerve palsy (wristdrop).
claims.quote: Typical symptoms of radial nerve palsy include wristdrop (weakness of the wrist and finger extensors) and sensory loss in the dorsal aspect of the first dorsal interosseous muscle. C7 radiculopathy can cause similar motor deficits.

claims.text: Median nerve roots: a lateral root from the lateral cord (C5, C6, C7) and a medial root from the medial cord (C8, T1).
claims.quote: lateral root: lateral cord of the brachial plexus (C5, C6, C7) medial root: medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8, T1)

claims.text: Median nerve course in the arm: lateral to the axillary artery, then down between biceps brachii and triceps brachii, crossing the brachial artery from lateral to medial; in the cubital fossa it lies medial to the brachial artery and the biceps tendon.
claims.quote: In the axilla, the median nerve lies lateral to the axillary artery. It enters the arm from axilla at the inferior margin of the teres major muscle and descends medially between biceps brachii and triceps brachii. In the arm, the median nerve courses laterally to the brachial artery and then crosses it, usually anteriorly, from lateral to medial. It lies initially on coracobrachialis, then brachialis. In the cubital fossa, the median nerve lies medial to the brachial artery and the biceps brachii tendon.

claims.text: Median nerve in the forearm and wrist: enters the forearm between the two heads of pronator teres (giving off the anterior interosseous nerve), runs between flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, gives off the palmar cutaneous branch about 5 cm above the wrist, and is the only nerve through the carpal tunnel, deep to the flexor retinaculum.
claims.quote: The median nerve leaves the bicipital aponeurosis and enters the forearm between the two heads of pronator teres muscle and gives off the anterior interosseous nerve. It courses towards the wrist deep to flexor digitorum superficialis and superficial to flexor digitorum profundus muscle. It emerges lateral to the flexor digitorum superficialis about 5 cm proximal to the wrist (giving off the palmar cutaneous branch) and enters the hand through the carpal tunnel (the only nerve to traverse the carpal tunnel), passing deep to the flexor retinaculum at the wrist.

claims.text: Median nerve motor supply: every anterior forearm flexor and pronator except flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus; in the hand, the thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals.
claims.quote: all the muscles (flexor and pronator) of anterior compartment of the forearm except flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar half of FDP in the hand the thenar muscles (as described above) and the lateral two lumbricals

claims.text: Anterior interosseous nerve: flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus and the radial half of flexor digitorum profundus.
claims.quote: anterior interosseous nerve: supplies flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus and radial half of flexor digitorum profundus

claims.text: Median nerve sensory supply: skin over the thenar eminence and the palmar thumb, index, middle finger and radial half of the ring finger.
claims.quote: sensory supply: skin over thenar eminence, palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle finger and radial half of the ring finger

claims.text: Carpal tunnel signs: radial-palmar hand paresthesias and wrist and palm pain (may radiate to the forearm and shoulder, may be worse at night); later sensory loss over the palmar first 3 fingers and weak, atrophied thumb abduction and opposition.
claims.quote: The compression causes paresthesias in the radial-palmar aspect of the hand and pain in the wrist and palm. Pain may be referred to the forearm and shoulder. Pain may be more severe at night. A sensory deficit in the palmar aspect of the first 3 fingers may follow, and the muscles that control thumb abduction and opposition may become weak and atrophied.

claims.text: Carpal tunnel risk factors: pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, some forms of amyloidosis, rheumatoid arthritis and repeated forceful work with the wrist extended; most cases are idiopathic.
claims.quote: Risk factors for carpal tunnel syndrome include Pregnancy Diabetes Hypothyroidism Certain forms of amyloidosis Rheumatoid arthritis Work that requires repeated forceful movements with the wrist extended (eg, using a screwdriver) Possibly use of a computer keyboard that is not positioned correctly (controversial) However, most cases are idiopathic.

claims.text: Ulnar nerve origin: a terminal branch of the medial cord, from C8–T1.
claims.quote: The ulnar nerve originates as a terminal branch of the medial cord of the brachial plexus with nerve root fibers from the ventral rami of C8-T1.

claims.text: Ulnar nerve course in the arm: medial to the axillary and brachial arteries, through the medial intermuscular septum (arcade of Struthers) into the posterior compartment, then behind the medial epicondyle in the cubital tunnel.
claims.quote: In the arm, the ulnar nerve runs medial to the axillary artery and subsequently the brachial artery on the coracobrachialis muscle in the anterior compartment of the arm. The nerve passes into the posterior compartment through the medial intermuscular septum, piercing the arcade of Struthers running distally with the superior ulnar collateral artery. Further on, it runs between the medial head of the triceps brachii muscle and the medial intermuscular septum to pass posterior to the medial humeral epicondyle in the superficial condylar groove (cubital tunnel).

claims.text: Ulnar nerve in the forearm: enters between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, runs deep to it on flexor digitorum profundus, medial to the ulnar artery.
claims.quote: The ulnar nerve enters the forearm from the arm in between the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) muscle. It subsequently lies superficial to flexor digitorum profundus, deep to FCU and medial to the ulnar artery. It courses distally along the ulnar aspect of the forearm and at the wrist, the ulnar nerve runs lateral to the tendon of FCU.

claims.text: Ulnar nerve at the wrist: gives off the dorsal cutaneous branch before the wrist, then enters the hand superficial to the flexor retinaculum in Guyon's canal with the ulnar artery and vein.
claims.quote: Prior to passing the flexor retinaculum at the wrist, the ulnar nerve gives off the dorsal cutaneous branch. The ulnar nerve enters the hand superficial to the flexor retinaculum and inside Guyon's canal traveling with the ulnar artery and vein.

claims.text: Ulnar nerve motor supply: flexor carpi ulnaris, medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, the hypothenar muscles, 3rd and 4th lumbricals, palmar and dorsal interossei, deep head of flexor pollicis brevis, adductor pollicis and palmaris brevis.
claims.quote: motor flexor carpi ulnaris flexor digitorum profundus (medial half) hypothenar muscles (abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi brevis, opponens digiti minimi) 3rd and 4th lumbricals palmar and dorsal interossei muscles flexor pollicis brevis (deep head) adductor pollicis palmaris brevis

claims.text: Ulnar nerve sensory supply: medial palm, palmar and dorsal fifth digit, and the adjacent half of the fourth digit.
claims.quote: sensory supply: medial aspect of the palm, the palmar and dorsal aspects of the fifth digit, and the adjacent half of the fourth digit

claims.text: Ulnar compression at the elbow: paresthesias and sensory loss in the fifth digit and medial half of the fourth; weak, possibly atrophied thumb adductor, fifth-digit abductor and interosseous muscles.
claims.quote: Compression at the level of the elbow can cause paresthesias and a sensory deficit in the fifth digit and medial half of the fourth digit; the thumb adductor, fifth digit abductor, and interosseus muscles are weak and may be atrophied.

claims.text: Cubital tunnel: the ulnar nerve can be compressed where it runs under the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel (cubital tunnel syndrome).
claims.quote: The ulnar nerve can also be compressed as it runs under the medial epicondyle through tissue forming the cubital tunnel (sometimes causing cubital tunnel syndrome).

claims.text: Pressure palsies: prolonged pressure at bony prominences usually affects superficial nerves (ulnar, radial, peroneal), especially in thin people, e.g. during sound sleep, intoxication, bicycle riding or anesthesia.
claims.quote: Prolonged, uninterrupted pressure at bony prominences can cause pressure neuropathy, usually affecting superficial nerves (ulnar, radial, peroneal), particularly in thin people; such pressure may occur during sound sleep, intoxication, bicycle riding, or anesthesia.
